prompt_sources.problem:
The set $\{{\mathbf{a}}_{\mathbf{1}},{\mathbf{a}}_{\mathbf{2}}\}$ is linearly dependent. Which of the following vectors could be ${\mathbf{a}}_{2}$ if
${\mathbf{a}}_{\mathbf{1}}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -3\end{aligned}]?$

solution_sources.worked_solution:
We say that two vectors ${\mathbf{v}}_{1}$ and ${\mathbf{v}}_{2}$ are *linearly independent* if the only solution to the equation

$$
{x}_{1}{\mathbf{v}}_{1}+{x}_{2}{\mathbf{v}}_{2}=\mathbf{0}
$$

is ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}=0.$ Otherwise, the vectors are *linearly dependent*.

A set containing *only two* vectors is linearly *dependent* if and only if the two vectors are parallel.

From the given options, the correct answer is 

$$
{\mathbf{a}}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-8 \\ 12\end{aligned}].
$$

To see why, notice that 

$$
[\begin{aligned}-8 \\ 12\end{aligned}]=-4[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -3\end{aligned}]=-4{\mathbf{a}}_{1}.
$$

This way, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}4{\mathbf{a}}_{1}-4{\mathbf{a}}_{1} & =\mathbf{0} \\ 4{\mathbf{a}}_{1}+{\mathbf{a}}_{2} & =\mathbf{0}.\end{aligned}
$$

In other words, the vectors ${\mathbf{a}}_{1}$ and ${\mathbf{a}}_{2}$ are parallel.

To see why this means that ${\mathbf{a}}_{1}$ and ${\mathbf{a}}_{2}$ are linearly dependent, we notice that the equation

$$
{x}_{1}{\mathbf{a}}_{1}+{x}_{2}{\mathbf{a}}_{2}=\mathbf{0}
$$

has the solution ${x}_{1}=4$ and ${x}_{2}=1,$ which is different from ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}=0.$ Therefore, the set is linearly dependent.

solution_sources.worked_solution:
We say that two vectors ${\mathbf{v}}_{1}$ and ${\mathbf{v}}_{2}$ are *linearly independent* if the only solution to the equation

$$
{x}_{1}{\mathbf{v}}_{1}+{x}_{2}{\mathbf{v}}_{2}=\mathbf{0}
$$

is ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}=0.$ Otherwise, the vectors are *linearly dependent*.

A set containing *only two* vectors is linearly *dependent* if and only if the two vectors are parallel.

From the given options, the correct answer is 

$$
{\mathbf{a}}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ -20 \\ 10\end{aligned}].
$$

To see why, notice that 

$$
[\begin{aligned}5 \\ -20 \\ 10\end{aligned}]=5[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -4 \\ 2\end{aligned}]=5{\mathbf{a}}_{1}.
$$

This way, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}5{\mathbf{a}}_{1}-5{\mathbf{a}}_{1} & =\mathbf{0} \\ 5{\mathbf{a}}_{1}-{\mathbf{a}}_{2} & =\mathbf{0} \\ 5{\mathbf{a}}_{1}+(-1){\mathbf{a}}_{2} & =\mathbf{0}.\end{aligned}
$$

In other words, the vectors ${\mathbf{a}}_{1}$ and ${\mathbf{a}}_{2}$ are parallel.

To see why this means that ${\mathbf{a}}_{1}$ and ${\mathbf{a}}_{2}$ are linearly dependent, notice that the equation

$$
{x}_{1}{\mathbf{a}}_{1}+{x}_{2}{\mathbf{a}}_{2}=\mathbf{0}
$$

has the solution ${x}_{1}=5$ and ${x}_{2}=-1,$ which is different from ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}=0.$ Therefore, the set is linearly dependent.

We say that two vectors ${\mathbf{v}}_{1}$ and ${\mathbf{v}}_{2}$ are *linearly independent* if the only solution to the equation

$$
{x}_{1}{\mathbf{v}}_{1}+{x}_{2}{\mathbf{v}}_{2}=\mathbf{0}
$$

is ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}=0.$ Otherwise, the vectors are *linearly dependent*.

A set containing *only two* vectors is linearly *dependent* if and only if the two vectors are parallel.

From the given options, the correct answer is

$$
{\mathbf{a}}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -6\end{aligned}].
$$

To see why, notice that 

$$
[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -6\end{aligned}]=(-2)[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]=-2{\mathbf{a}}_{1}.
$$

This way, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}2{\mathbf{a}}_{1}-2{\mathbf{a}}_{1} & =\mathbf{0} \\ 2{\mathbf{a}}_{1}+{\mathbf{a}}_{2} & =\mathbf{0}.\end{aligned}
$$

In other words, the vectors ${\mathbf{a}}_{1}$ and ${\mathbf{a}}_{2}$ are parallel.

To see why this means that ${\mathbf{a}}_{1}$ and ${\mathbf{a}}_{2}$ are linearly dependent, we notice that the equation

$$
{x}_{1}{\mathbf{a}}_{1}+{x}_{2}{\mathbf{a}}_{2}=\mathbf{0}
$$

has the solution ${x}_{1}=2$ and ${x}_{2}=1,$ which is different from ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}=0.$ Therefore, the set is linearly dependent.

We say that two vectors ${\mathbf{v}}_{1}$ and ${\mathbf{v}}_{2}$ are *linearly independent* if the only solution to the equation

$$
{x}_{1}{\mathbf{v}}_{1}+{x}_{2}{\mathbf{v}}_{2}=\mathbf{0}
$$

is ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}=0.$ Otherwise, the vectors are *linearly dependent*.

A set containing *only two* vectors is linearly *dependent* if and only if the two vectors are parallel.

From the given options, the correct answer is 

$$
{\mathbf{a}}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ -3 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

 

To see why, notice that 

$$
[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ -3 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=-\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}8 \\ 6 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=-\frac{1}{2}{\mathbf{a}}_{1}.
$$

This way, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{\mathbf{a}}_{1}-\frac{1}{2}{\mathbf{a}}_{1} & =\mathbf{0} \\ \frac{1}{2}{\mathbf{a}}_{1}+{\mathbf{a}}_{2} & =\mathbf{0}\end{aligned}
$$

In other words, the vectors ${\mathbf{a}}_{1}$ and ${\mathbf{a}}_{2}$ are parallel.

To see why this means that ${\mathbf{a}}_{1}$ and ${\mathbf{a}}_{2}$ are linearly dependent, we notice that the equation

$$
{x}_{1}{\mathbf{a}}_{1}+{x}_{2}{\mathbf{a}}_{2}=\mathbf{0}
$$

has the solution ${x}_{1}=\frac{1}{2}$ and ${x}_{2}=1,$ which is different from ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}=0.$ Therefore, the set is linearly dependent.

We say that two vectors ${\mathbf{v}}_{1}$ and ${\mathbf{v}}_{2}$ are *linearly independent* if the only solution to the equation

$$
{x}_{1}{\mathbf{v}}_{1}+{x}_{2}{\mathbf{v}}_{2}=\mathbf{0}
$$

is ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}=0.$ Otherwise, the vectors are *linearly dependent*.

A set containing *only two* vectors is linearly *dependent* if and only if the two vectors are parallel.

From the given options, the correct answer is 

$$
{\mathbf{a}}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-10 \\ -2 \\ 4\end{aligned}].
$$

To see why, notice that 

$$
[\begin{aligned}-10 \\ -2 \\ 4\end{aligned}]=(-2)[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 1 \\ -2\end{aligned}]=-2{\mathbf{a}}_{1}.
$$

This way, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}2{\mathbf{a}}_{1}-2{\mathbf{a}}_{1} & =\mathbf{0} \\ 2{\mathbf{a}}_{1}+{\mathbf{a}}_{2} & =\mathbf{0}\end{aligned}
$$

In other words, the vectors ${\mathbf{a}}_{1}$ and ${\mathbf{a}}_{2}$ are parallel.

To see why this means that ${\mathbf{a}}_{1}$ and ${\mathbf{a}}_{2}$ are linearly dependent, we notice that the equation

$$
{x}_{1}{\mathbf{a}}_{1}+{x}_{2}{\mathbf{a}}_{2}=\mathbf{0}
$$

has the solution ${x}_{1}=2$ and ${x}_{2}=1,$ which is different from ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}=0.$ Therefore, the set is linearly dependent.

We say that two vectors ${\mathbf{v}}_{1}$ and ${\mathbf{v}}_{2}$ are *linearly independent* if the only solution to the equation

$$
{x}_{1}{\mathbf{v}}_{1}+{x}_{2}{\mathbf{v}}_{2}=\mathbf{0}
$$

is ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}=0.$ Otherwise, the vectors are *linearly dependent*.

A set containing *only two* vectors is linearly *dependent* if and only if the two vectors are parallel.

From the given options, the correct answer is

$$
{\mathbf{a}}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3 \\ -4\end{aligned}].
$$

To see why, notice that 

$$
[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3 \\ -4\end{aligned}]=-\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -6 \\ 8\end{aligned}]=-\frac{1}{2}{\mathbf{a}}_{1}.
$$

This way, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{\mathbf{a}}_{1}-\frac{1}{2}{\mathbf{a}}_{1} & =\mathbf{0} \\ \frac{1}{2}{\mathbf{a}}_{1}+{\mathbf{a}}_{2} & =\mathbf{0}\end{aligned}
$$

In other words, the vectors ${\mathbf{a}}_{1}$ and ${\mathbf{a}}_{2}$ are parallel.

To see why this means that ${\mathbf{a}}_{1}$ and ${\mathbf{a}}_{2}$ are linearly dependent, we notice that the equation

$$
{x}_{1}{\mathbf{a}}_{1}+{x}_{2}{\mathbf{a}}_{2}=\mathbf{0}
$$

has the solution ${x}_{1}=\frac{1}{2}$ and ${x}_{2}=1,$ which is different from ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}=0.$ Therefore, the set is linearly dependent.

We say that two vectors ${\mathbf{v}}_{1}$ and ${\mathbf{v}}_{2}$ are *linearly independent* if the only solution to the equation

$$
{x}_{1}{\mathbf{v}}_{1}+{x}_{2}{\mathbf{v}}_{2}=\mathbf{0}
$$

is ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}=0.$ Otherwise, the vectors are *linearly dependent*.

A set containing *only two* vectors is linearly *dependent* if and only if the two vectors are parallel.

From the given options, the correct answer is 

$$
{\mathbf{a}}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}20 \\ -8\end{aligned}].
$$

To see why, notice that 

$$
[\begin{aligned}20 \\ -8\end{aligned}]=4[\begin{aligned}5 \\ -2\end{aligned}]=4{\mathbf{a}}_{1}.
$$

This way, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}4{\mathbf{a}}_{1}-4{\mathbf{a}}_{1} & =\mathbf{0} \\ 4{\mathbf{a}}_{1}-{\mathbf{a}}_{2} & =\mathbf{0} \\ 4{\mathbf{a}}_{1}+(-1){\mathbf{a}}_{2} & =\mathbf{0}.\end{aligned}
$$

In other words, the vectors ${\mathbf{a}}_{1}$ and ${\mathbf{a}}_{2}$ are parallel.

To see why this means that ${\mathbf{a}}_{1}$ and ${\mathbf{a}}_{2}$ are linearly dependent, we notice that the equation

$$
{x}_{1}{\mathbf{a}}_{1}+{x}_{2}{\mathbf{a}}_{2}=\mathbf{0}
$$

has the solution ${x}_{1}=4$ and ${x}_{2}=-1,$ which is different from ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}=0.$ Therefore, the set is linearly dependent.

$$
{x}_{1}{\mathbf{v}}_{1}+{x}_{2}{\mathbf{v}}_{2}=\mathbf{0}
$$

$$

This way, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}2{\mathbf{a}}_{1}-2{\mathbf{a}}_{1} & =\mathbf{0} \\ 2{\mathbf{a}}_{1}+{\mathbf{a}}_{2} & =\mathbf{0}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{x}_{1}{\mathbf{a}}_{1}+{x}_{2}{\mathbf{a}}_{2}=\mathbf{0}

prompt_sources.problem:
Consider the following vectors:

$$
{\mathbf{a}}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,{\mathbf{a}}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{\mathbf{a}}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Which of the following statements are true?

I. $2{\mathbf{a}}_{1}-{\mathbf{a}}_{2}+{\mathbf{a}}_{3}=\mathbf{0}.$

II. ${x}_{1}{\mathbf{a}}_{1}+{x}_{2}{\mathbf{a}}_{2}+{x}_{3}{\mathbf{a}}_{3}=\mathbf{0}$ only if ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}={x}_{3}=0.$

III. The set $\{{\mathbf{a}}_{1},{\mathbf{a}}_{2},{\mathbf{a}}_{3}\}$ is linearly independent.

solution_sources.worked_solution:
We say that three vectors ${\mathbf{v}}_{1},{\mathbf{v}}_{2}$ and ${\mathbf{v}}_{3}$ are *linearly independent* if the only solution to the equation

$$
{x}_{1}{\mathbf{v}}_{1}+{x}_{2}{\mathbf{v}}_{2}+{x}_{3}{\mathbf{v}}_{3}=\mathbf{0}
$$

is ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}={x}_{3}=0.$ Otherwise, the vectors are *linearly dependent*.

With that in mind, let's look at each statement in turn.

- Statement I is false. Indeed:

$$
\begin{aligned}2{\mathbf{a}}_{1}-{\mathbf{a}}_{2}+{\mathbf{a}}_{3} & =2[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2 \\ 4\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2-3+1 \\ -2-0+2 \\ 4-0+0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\  & \ne \mathbf{0}\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is true. The equation ${x}_{1}{\mathbf{a}}_{1}+{x}_{2}{\mathbf{a}}_{2}+{x}_{3}{\mathbf{a}}_{3}=\mathbf{0}$ corresponds to the system

$$
\begin{cases}{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}=0 \\ -{x}_{1}+2{x}_{3}=0 \\ 2{x}_{1}=0.\end{cases}
$$

Solving this system using back substitution, we find that the solution is ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}={x}_{3}=0.$

- Statement III is true. Since statement II is true, the set $\{{\mathbf{a}}_{1},{\mathbf{a}}_{2},{\mathbf{a}}_{3}\}$ is linearly independent.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only."

Assume that $x_1,x_2,$ and $x_3$ are real numbers. Which of the following statements are true?

I. The equation $x_1\mathbf{a}_1+x_2\mathbf{a}_2+x_3\mathbf{a}_3=\mathbf{0}$ has an infinite number of nonzero solutions.

II. The vectors $\mathbf{a}_1,\mathbf{a}_2,$ and $\mathbf{a}_3$ are linearly independent.

III. The vectors $\mathbf{a}_1,\mathbf{a}_2,$ and $\mathbf{a}_3$ are linearly dependent.
solution_sources.worked_solution:
We say that three vectors $\mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2,$ and $\mathbf{v}_3$ are *linearly independent* if the only solution to the equation

$$
x_1 \mathbf{v}_1 + x_2 \mathbf{v}_2 + x_3 \mathbf{v}_3 = \mathbf{0}
$$

is $x_1 = x_2 = x_3 = 0.$ Otherwise, the vectors are *linearly dependent*.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

The equation $x_1\mathbf{a}_1+x_2\mathbf{a}_2+x_3\mathbf{a}_3=\mathbf{0}$ corresponds to the system

$$
\begin{cases}2{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}+2{x}_{3}=0 \\ 4{x}_{1}+4{x}_{2}+5{x}_{3}=0 \\ 6{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}=0.\end{cases}
$$

To solve the system, we create its augmented matrix and reduce it using Gaussian elimination:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{array}{ccc|c}2 & -1 & 2 & 0 \\ 4 & 4 & 5 & 0 \\ 0 & 6 & 1 & 0\end{array}] & {R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{array}{ccc|c}2 & -1 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 6 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 6 & 1 & 0\end{array}] & {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-1){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{array}{ccc|c}2 & -1 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 6 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{array}]\end{aligned}
$$

From the matrix above, we conclude that the basic variables are $x_1$ and $x_2,$ while $x_3$ is the free variable. 

Since there is one free variable, the equation $x_1\mathbf{a}_1+x_2\mathbf{a}_2+x_3\mathbf{a}_3=\mathbf{0}$ has an infinite number of nonzero solutions, which means that the vectors are linearly dependent. 

Therefore, statements II is false, while statements I and III are true.
